lecture_context.lecture_title: What’s Going On Inside My Model?

unit.name: Data diagnostics, MoE routing metrics, and closing Q&A
unit.description: Explains data-distribution checks, token statistics, contamination checks, MoE router monitoring, and Q&A on domain mixtures and synthetic data.
unit.summary: Data diagnostics are presented as a final frontier-model lens, with distribution checks over domains such as law, Wikipedia, Stack Exchange, and GitHub used to understand where loss or performance may shift [ts=5555s] [ts=5596s]. The instructor connects underrepresented domains to likely performance drops and suggests sampling methods, analogous to experience replay, to maintain stable domain frequencies through training [ts=5623s] [ts=5640s] [ts=5696s]. Token statistics are another signal: changes in important tokens, such as math symbols or non-English tokens, can explain regressions or distribution shifts [ts=5723s] [ts=5801s]. The summary dashboard includes global/domain losses, scaling alignment, MoE router use and load balancing, gradient norms, learning rates, checkpoint-to-checkpoint evals, benchmark behavior, token distribution, and tokenizer statistics [ts=5826s] [ts=5850s] [ts=5905s]. Q&A revisits domain mixtures and synthetic data, emphasizing that neighboring domains can help but too much cheap synthetic data can distort token frequencies and hurt other domains [ts=5945s] [ts=6120s].

key_points.text: Distribution checks track domain proportions in the training data and can reveal domain-specific performance shifts.
If a domain is underrepresented in the data, performance on that domain is likely to drop relative to others.
Sampling methods can help maintain stable domain frequencies across different portions of training.
Token statistics monitor frequency changes for key tokens, such as math symbols, that can affect task performance.
MoE router metrics help detect whether routing collapses onto the same experts or underuses specialized experts.
Frontier-lab dashboards often include losses, scaling alignment, router metrics, gradient norms, learning rates, benchmark results, token distribution, and tokenizer statistics.
Synthetic data can be useful for augmentation, but overusing cheap synthetic data in one domain can distort token frequencies and harm performance elsewhere.
